<reason>B (PRO) won a high-quality, closely fought debate by answering the hardest pressure more directly and tying its case more cleanly to the motion's actual decision rule. A's opening attack — that B's showcase examples were competitively chosen elites, so the block grant was "the prize, not the selection mechanism" — was excellent and forced real work. But B's answers to both pressure questions were decisive: the backward-looking evidence assessment of people versus forward-looking prophecy of ideas dissolved A's "why trust consensus for people but not ideas" gotcha, and B supplied a concrete scaled mechanism (base allocation plus retrospective external redistribution, UK-style core funding, Max Planck closures) rather than hand-waving. B also flipped A's best exhibit: Karikó was rejected by public competition for a decade and rescued by industry, which exists under either system — A's counter that industry is a door "only a project-based ecosystem creates" was an overclaim. Because the motion pre-concedes the accountability cost, A's retreat to procedural virtues (rotation, appeal, visibility) was partly priced out, and A never rebuilt the claim that competition funds daring ideas after B's preliminary-data/consensus-averaging attacks. A's incumbency and error-correction framing ("competition errs with redundancy; block grants err alone") stayed live and kept the debate competitive. B's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a real but minor execution cost since its substance landed elsewhere.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's A1 in Rebuttal 2: judging a person is backward-looking assessment of a demonstrated record while judging a project is forward prophecy that outliers necessarily fail, plus the asymmetry that CON's system runs both filters — it turned A's sharpest pressure question into a strengthening of B's case. Runner-up: the Karikó flip ("CON's best exhibit for competition is a woman competition failed"), which A never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
